summary: XMPP identifies users with Jabber IDs, while LDAP is often used for white pages directory services. This document defines an LDAP schema that lets an XMPP address be stored in a user's directory entry.

eli5.summary: It adds a spot for a person's chat address in the company phone book, so you can look them up and message them.

questions: how to store xmpp addresses in ldap
subtitle: How to store XMPP addresses in your company directory

tldr.problem: XMPP users are identified by Jabber IDs, but company directories (LDAP) traditionally store email and phone numbers, not chat addresses. There was no standard way to link them together.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a small LDAP schema addition: a JID attribute and a JIDObject auxiliary object class that lets any directory entry include an XMPP address.
tldr.outcome: Now LDAP directories like corporate address books can store Jabber IDs, making it easy to look up people by their chat identities alongside other contact info.

today: RFC 8284 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the standard for how LDAP directories include XMPP contact information.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) is a protocol for instant messaging and presence information that identifies users by Jabber IDs (JIDs). Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is a protocol for white pages services—online directories that store information about users and resources, organized by schema that relates to users and support for Internet protocols.

The RFC defines a schema that enables XMPP JIDs to be stored in LDAP directory objects. This allows white pages applications to use both the JID and other user information together when serving lookups.
sections.eli5: XMPP uses addresses to find people; LDAP stores address books. This spec adds a way to put your XMPP address in the address book.

sections.title: Conventions and Definitions
sections.content: The document uses standard RFC terminology from BCP 14 for requirements levels. Key words like MUST, SHOULD, and MAY are used as defined in RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 to describe whether implementations must, should, or may follow specific behaviors.
sections.eli5: The document follows the standard rules for how RFCs describe what things must happen and what's optional.

sections.title: Schema Definition
sections.content:
The schema adds two components to LDAP: an auxiliary object class called JIDObject and an attribute called jid. The JIDObject class may be associated with any structural object class in the directory. This design lets the JID attribute be added to existing directory entries without replacing their primary object class. The JID attribute is optional, which allows an entry to be configured to hold a JID but contain none currently.

The JID attribute stores an XMPP address using Directory String syntax and case-insensitive matching. The stored JID must be a bare JID (such as romeo@shakespeare.example.com representing a human user), not a full JID with a resource identifier (such as romeo@shakespeare.example.com/AABBCC, which represents a specific client instance). The RFC notes that while the directory server is not expected to enforce JID syntax rules, XMPP applications reading the attribute should validate the values according to RFC 7622.
sections.eli5: The schema adds a slot called 'jid' where you can put someone's XMPP address. You can add this slot to any kind of person or thing stored in the directory. The slot is optional—you can set it up but not fill it in yet.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers two object identifiers with IANA under the Internet Directory Numbers registry. The JIDObject object class is registered with OID 1.3.6.1.1.23.1, and the jid attribute is registered with OID 1.3.6.1.1.23.2. Both fall under the XMPP (decimal 23) branch in the Internet Directory Numbers hierarchy. These registrations ensure that LDAP implementations can use consistent identifiers when implementing this schema.
sections.eli5: The spec gets official registration numbers from IANA so everyone uses the same identifiers when adding XMPP info to directories.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
XMPP JIDs function as personal identifiers that enable electronic communication, much like email addresses. Publishing JID information in LDAP directories—which may be corporate or public services—requires care to protect privacy. Organizations should only publish JID information that individuals have consented to and that is appropriate to make accessible to all LDAP users.

Beyond the JID-specific considerations, all the general security recommendations from RFC 4510 (the LDAP Technical Specification) apply. These include access control, authentication, and secure communication between clients and servers.
sections.eli5: XMPP addresses are personal information, like email. Be careful about who gets to see them in your directory, and follow the normal rules for keeping LDAP safe.
